Delimiters stayed balanced, so the imbalance probe passed it. out/verify.mjs now checks for control characters directly.

answer:
**(D)**

Negate the conjunction first, by De Morgan's law:

\(\sim [p \land (q \rightarrow r)] \equiv \sim p \vee \sim (q \rightarrow r)\)

Now negate the implication. Since \(q \rightarrow r \equiv \sim q \vee r\), its negation is \(\sim (\sim q \vee r) \equiv q \land \sim r\). Substituting:

\(\equiv \sim p \vee (q \land \sim r)\)

which is option (D). The three distractors each go wrong at one step: (A) drops the negation on \(p\), (B) leaves the implication un-negated, and (C) negates the implication as though it were another implication.

**(C)** — but see the note below; this question is defective as printed.

By De Morgan's law, and using \(\sim (q \rightarrow r) \equiv q \land \sim r\):

\(\sim [p \land (q \rightarrow r)] \equiv \sim p \vee (q \land \sim r)\)

No printed option is this expression — the combination \((q \land \sim r)\) appears in none of the four. Option (C) reads \(\sim p \vee (q \rightarrow \sim r)\), which is the correct answer with a single connective mis-set, so it is the intended key.

**(B)** \(T,\ F\)

Work from the stronger condition. \(p \rightarrow q\) is false in exactly one case — a true antecedent with a false consequent — so \(p \equiv T\) and \(q \equiv F\).

Check this against the other condition: \(p \land q \equiv T \land F \equiv F\), as required. Both hold, so the truth values are \(T,\ F\).

| \(p\) | \(q\) | \(p \land q\) | \(p \rightarrow q\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | T |
| T | F | F | F |
| F | T | F | T |
| F | F | F | T |

Only the second row makes both columns \(F\).

**(B)** \(c \land (p \land q)\)

The dual of a statement is obtained by interchanging \(\land\) with \(\vee\), and \(t\) (tautology) with \(c\) (contradiction), leaving the variables and their negations unchanged.

Applying this to \(t \vee (p \vee q)\): the leading \(t\) becomes \(c\), and both occurrences of \(\vee\) become \(\land\), giving

\(c \land (p \land q)\)

Options (C) and (D) keep \(t\) instead of replacing it, and (A) changes only the outer connective.

**(C)**

Test each statement against \(A = \{1,2,3,4,5\}\).

- (A) \(\exists x \in A\) with \(x + 3 = 8\): take \(x = 5\). **True.**
- (B) \(\exists x \in A\) with \(x + 2 < 9\): take \(x = 1\), giving \(3 < 9\). **True.**
- (C) \(\forall x \in A,\ x + 6 \geq 9\): this one is universal, so a single counterexample defeats it. At \(x = 1\), \(x + 6 = 7\), and \(7 \geq 9\) is false. **False.**
- (D) \(\exists x \in A\) with \(x + 6 < 10\): take \(x = 1\), giving \(7 < 10\). **True.**

(C) is the only false statement, and it is also the only universally-quantified one: an existential claim needs a single witness, a universal claim must survive every element.
